newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - Chirac says no doubt Spain to join EMU in 1999.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Chirac says no doubt Spain to join EMU in 1999.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac said on Tuesday he had no doubt Spain would join a single European currrency in 1999 and would also like to see Italy joining monetary union at the same time.

He told a news conference after a Franco-Spanish summit in this Mediterranean port city that he was impressed by Spain's determined and "courageous" efforts to prepare its economy for Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).

"We have no doubt as regards (to) Spain. Italy has shown the same determination. We would like Italy to be ready with the others," he said in response to a question about whether he thought Spain could join EMU in 1999 without fellow Mediterranean state and founding European Union member Italy.

Last month, Chirac sparked a diplomatic row with Rome when he suggested Italy might not be ready in time to join a single currency, a view held by many private economists who say Italy is trailing Spain in its preparations for EMU.
He has since switched to a message of hope that Italy, which plans a special "euro" tax to cut its public deficit, will join the first group of countries joining EMU from the start.

Spanish Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar also said he hoped Italy would join at the start. He added that Spain wanted the biggest number of countries possible to take part in 1999, provided the countries met Maastricht treaty criteria.
"We would like Italian participation from the start," he told the news conference.
Chirac also said he expected negotiations on the lira's re-entry to the European Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM), seen as a pre-condition to joining EMU, to be completed before year-end.
But a finance ministry source said since Italy had not yet made a formal request to bring the lira into the ERM, official negotiations had not yet started.
Despite this, most European officials say they still expect the lira to rejoin the ERM by the end of this year.

EMU participation by the Mediterranean countries of Spain, Italy and Portugal could play a crucial role in determining the nature of the single currency, the euro, after its launch and the monetary policies of the new monetary union.

Some economists say their participation may weaken the fledgling currency, which would then force the future European Central Bank to impose high interest rates on all countries in the euro zone to establish its credibiltiy and underpin the stability of the new currency.

All three countries have unveiled 1997 budgets designed to bring their public deficits down to three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) next year, the key year for deciding which countries qualify to join EMU in 1999.

Their efforts to meet Maastricht treaty criteria ran counter to expectations by some economists and politicians that the Mediterrenean countries would wait to join monetary union at a later stage once their economies were ready.
Europe's leaders are due to decide in early 1998, on the basis of fiscal and monetary performances in 1997, which countries can join a single currency at the launch in 1999.
